    The domain of every spot

    Source: R/result.R
    domains.Rd

    domains(fit) returns the result of sigdots() as a table with one row per spot, in the order of the input data, so that it can be joined to any other per-spot information (the true layers, cell types, a plot). For a Seurat or SpatialExperiment object, add_domains() does this joining for you.

    Usage

    domains(fit)

    Arguments

    fit

    A result of sigdots().

    Value

    A data frame with one row per spot and three columns:

    • spot: the spot identifier (the row name of the expression matrix, or the row number when there are no row names);

    • domain: the number of the domain the spot belongs to, 1, 2, ... in the order of the split tree from left to right (as printed by print(fit)). NA for a spot in a part of the tree that could not be tested (see summary(fit) and the warning given at the end of the run);

    • candidate_domain: the candidate domain the spot was in before the tests (its number, or your own label when candidate_labels was given).

    Details

    The domains are numbered by their position in the split tree, from left to right as print(fit) draws it, not by size. The spots of domain k are domains(fit)$spot[domains(fit)$domain == k].

    See also

    summary.sigdots() for the tests, plot.sigdots() for a map of the domains.

    Examples

    # \donttest{
fit <- sigdots(sigdots_example$x, sigdots_example$coords, K0 = 5, verbose = FALSE)
head(domains(fit))
#>      spot domain candidate_domain
#> 1 spot001      3                1
#> 2 spot002      3                1
#> 3 spot003      3                1
#> 4 spot004      3                5
#> 5 spot005      3                5
#> 6 spot006      3                5
table(domains(fit)$domain)
#> 
#>   1   2   3 
#> 300 300 300 
table(domain = domains(fit)$domain, true_region = sigdots_example$region)
#>       true_region
#> domain   1   2   3
#>      1   0   0 300
#>      2   0 300   0
#>      3 300   0   0
# }
